blocks.content: provisioner "local-exec" runs a command on the machine actually running Terraform itself, not on the resource being created, a genuinely important distinction that shapes everything else in this topic.
1. Full Depth, Starting Here

Provisioners were briefly introduced as a concept in the Core Concepts module, this module covers each one in complete, practical depth, starting with local-exec, genuinely the simplest of the three provisioners Terraform actually offers.

Everything covered across this five-topic module builds toward one honest conclusion, provisioners are real, useful tools in narrow, specific situations, and genuinely worth understanding well precisely so they can be used sparingly and deliberately.
That framing matters from the very first topic onward, because it is genuinely easy to reach for a provisioner out of familiarity, rather than because the situation actually calls for one.
Keep that in mind while reading through the concrete mechanics ahead, they are real and useful, but the honest goal of this module is knowing exactly when, and when not, to reach for them.

blocks.content: 2. Running on the Machine Running Terraform
blocks.text: 2. Running on the Machine Running Terraform

blocks.content: local-exec runs a real, actual shell command on whatever machine is executing terraform apply, your own laptop, or a CI runner, whichever that happens to be at that moment.

This matters because the command genuinely has access to whatever tools, credentials, and network reachability that specific machine already has, not whatever the newly created resource itself would have.
If a CI runner is what executes apply, that is also genuinely where the local-exec command runs, worth remembering when a script assumes tools or files that only exist on someone's personal laptop.
This single fact, where the command actually executes, is the one thing worth remembering above everything else in this topic, since it shapes every real use case that follows.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784539101132-919096119.png
blocks.alt: A command run on the machine running Terraform itself, wherever that actually is

blocks.content: 3. Not on the Resource Itself
This is genuinely worth being precise about, local-exec never runs anything on the real, newly-created resource, that is exactly the job of remote-exec, covered in the next topic.
Confusing the two is a genuinely common early mistake, expecting a local-exec command to somehow reach inside a fresh EC2 instance, when it never left the machine running Terraform at all.
A useful mental check is asking directly, does this command need to run where the resource itself lives, or somewhere else entirely, the answer immediately points to the right provisioner.

Holding this distinction clearly in mind before writing either provisioner avoids a genuinely frustrating class of debugging later, wondering why a command that clearly ran had no visible effect on the resource.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784539102968-749633908.png
blocks.alt: A genuinely important distinction, this never touches the real, new resource at all

4. When It Actually Fires
By default, a local-exec provisioner fires once, immediately after its owning resource finishes being created, part of the same real apply operation, not a separate, later step.
The optional on_failure argument controls what happens if the command itself fails, continue lets apply proceed anyway, fail, the default, stops and marks the resource tainted.

Choosing continue deliberately, for a genuinely non-critical side effect like a notification, avoids an entire apply failing over something that was never actually essential to the resource's own correctness.
Choosing the default fail behavior, for something that genuinely does matter, keeps a real problem visible immediately, rather than silently ignored and discovered much later.

blocks.content: 5. A Real Use Case: Generating a Local File
blocks.text: 5. A Real Use Case: Generating a Local File

blocks.content: Writing a newly created resource's real IP address, or ID, to a local inventory file for some other local tool to pick up afterward is a genuinely reasonable, common use of local-exec.
This kind of use case fits cleanly within local-exec's actual scope, a small, local side effect, rather than anything that needs to happen on the resource itself.
A genuinely common variant writes several resources' outputs into one combined file, useful as a lightweight handoff to another local tool or script in a broader pipeline.
Because this only ever touches the local machine, it is also one of the safer, more predictable provisioner use cases, with none of the network or SSH fragility covered later in this module.

blocks.content: 6. Referencing the Owning Resource
Inside a provisioner block, self.attribute refers directly to the owning resource's own attributes, exactly how the inventory example earlier reached self.public_ip.

This self reference is genuinely useful precisely because a provisioner is declared nested inside the resource it belongs to, letting it read that resource's freshly-computed, real attributes directly.
Without self, a provisioner would have no natural, direct way to reference values that only exist once its own owning resource has actually finished being created.
This is one of the small but genuinely important pieces of syntax that makes provisioners usable at all for anything beyond a fixed, static command.

blocks.content: 7. Choosing an Interpreter
The optional interpreter argument lets a command run through a specific shell or scripting interpreter, rather than the operating system's own default.
This genuinely matters on mixed teams, where the machine running Terraform might be Windows in one case and Linux in another, and the command needs to behave consistently either way.
Specifying interpreter explicitly removes a real, easy-to-miss source of inconsistency between different machines running the exact same configuration.
Without it, Terraform simply hands the command to the default shell, which is usually fine, but genuinely worth overriding whenever that default is not actually guaranteed.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784539112214-987671522.png
blocks.alt: A real, deliberate choice, over which shell or interpreter actually runs this command

blocks.content: 8. A Genuinely Common Mistake

A frequent, real mistake is relying on local-exec for something that genuinely should be tracked as real infrastructure state, a provisioner's side effects are invisible to Terraform's own state entirely.
If that local file, or that notification, is ever deleted or lost, Terraform has no way of knowing, and no way to recreate it on the next apply, since it was never part of state to begin with.
This is worth genuinely internalizing before relying on local-exec for anything beyond a clearly disposable, one-time side effect.
When in doubt, ask directly, would it matter if this silently never ran again, if the honest answer is yes, it likely belongs in real Terraform-managed state instead.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784539115259-180503668.png
blocks.alt: A real, genuine blind spot, Terraform's state never actually sees any of this

9. Idempotency Is Your Responsibility
Because local-exec commands are not tracked in state, Terraform has no built-in way to guarantee they behave safely if apply is genuinely run more than once against the same configuration.
That responsibility falls entirely on whatever the command itself actually does, a script appending to a file repeatedly, for instance, will genuinely keep growing that file on every single apply.
Writing local-exec commands defensively, checking before appending, or overwriting rather than appending, is a genuinely good habit worth building early.
This same idea, no built-in idempotency guarantee, resurfaces again later in this module, as one of the real, honest reasons provisioners are generally discouraged.

10. Debugging a Failing local-exec
When a local-exec command fails, its real output appears directly in the terraform apply output, genuinely the first, and often only, place worth looking.
Because the command runs locally, it is also possible, and genuinely useful, to copy that exact command out and run it directly in a terminal to reproduce and debug the failure faster.
This is a real, practical advantage over remote-exec, covered next, where reproducing a failure is genuinely more involved.
Keeping commands simple, and pushing anything genuinely complex into a real, separate script file, makes this kind of debugging noticeably easier.

blocks.text: 11. A Practical Checklist Before Using It

blocks.content: Before reaching for local-exec, working through a short, honest checklist genuinely helps confirm it is the right, deliberate choice for the situation at hand.

Confirm the command genuinely belongs on the local machine, not the resource itself, confirm on_failure reflects whether this side effect actually matters, and confirm the command behaves safely if it somehow runs more than once.

blocks.text: 12. How This Fits the Rest of the Module

blocks.content: local-exec is genuinely the simplest, and often the safest, of the three provisioners, precisely because it never touches the real, remote resource at all.
The next topic, remote-exec, raises the stakes considerably, running commands directly on real, live infrastructure, with everything that genuinely implies.
Keeping local-exec's relative simplicity in mind is a useful baseline while reading through remote-exec's real, additional requirements next.
Both provisioners share the same underlying honest philosophy this whole module builds toward, real tools, used deliberately, not by default.

With local-exec now covered in full, the next topic covers remote-exec, the provisioner that runs commands directly on the resource itself, the natural next step in this module.
The core distinction from this entire topic, where a command actually runs, carries forward directly, and is the single clearest way to choose between the two.
From here, this module continues building toward the file provisioner, and then the genuinely honest guidance on when any of the three actually belong in real, production configuration.
That honest through-line, understanding these tools well enough to use them sparingly, is worth carrying forward into every topic that follows.
